source.title: Fundamental safety-capability trade-offs in fine-tuning large language models
source.authors: Pin-Yu Chen; Han Shen; Payel Das; Tianyi Chen

record.file_problem: No apparent text corruption or truncation; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It empirically studies safety-capability effects of fine-tuning using loss-gap measures, a different measure from harmful-request refusal. It does not test the specific behaviors named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The experiments fine-tune an Orca-aligned Llama-2-7B and report safety alignment loss gaps and capability loss gaps. These are not harmful-request compliance or refusal rates, so the results are recorded under fits_no_version rather than linked to a claim version. The paper does not measure per-token KL, compliant-prefix or suffix bypasses, decoding changes, safety-localized parameters, or deepening interventions. Its own results are included; cited results are not.
record.test_reason: The paper takes the safety-capability trade-off from fine-tuning as given, citing Qi et al., and builds a theory of it. Its experiments never measure harmful-request compliance or refusal. The 'safety alignment' data is Orca, a general instruction dataset of summarization and reasoning tasks, not safety or refusal data. Its 'safety' measure is the loss gap on Orca after LoRA fine-tuning. This is a related but different construct, so no row bears on any version, and the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude, theoretically and on Llama-2-7B loss-gap experiments, that proxy-data similarity and context overlap govern the trade-off under an alignment-loss constraint. Under a parameter constraint, the local loss landscape governs it. The paraphrase should add that 'safety' is operationalized as loss on Orca instruction data, not refusal behaviour.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use benign task datasets and measure empirical safety and capability loss gaps, rather than harmful fine-tuning and harmful-request refusal. The paper also analyzes alignment-loss and parameter-neighborhood constraints.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss-gap outcomes vary with proxy safety-data similarity, context overlap between safety and task inputs, penalty strength λ, and parameter-neighborhood size ε2.

fits_no_version.finding: In Case I, proxy alignment data closer to the original alignment data (Alpaca-GPT-4 over Alpaca, and Orca itself) gives a lower loss gap on the original alignment data after LoRA fine-tuning of an Orca-tuned Llama-2-7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixing proxy alignment data more similar to the original alignment data better preserves the original alignment loss during fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Raising λ trades capability loss gap against alignment loss gap. Code fine-tuning data (Commitpackft), which has little input overlap with Orca, gives the smallest capability loss gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input-domain overlap between alignment and task data worsens the trade-off between alignment loss and capability loss.

fits_no_version.finding: A parameter-distance penalty (smaller ε2) lowers the alignment loss gap but yields a larger capability loss gap than the Case I loss-constraint approach.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraining parameters near the aligned model preserves alignment loss at a capability cost.

record.peer_reviewed: PNAS Nexus (venue stated in the supplied metadata)
record.problems: The reported experimental outcomes are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The safety metric is a loss gap on alignment data, not a direct harmful-request refusal or compliance rate; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Theorem statements and proofs (Sections 2.2–2.3 and 4.2–4.5) are theoretical bounds rather than model-level measured outcomes. No cited results from other work were recorded as rows.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning data and no harmful-request evaluation.
Fine-tunes on benign task data (Commitpackft, Alpaca, Open-platypus) but never measures harmful compliance or refusal. It reports only the loss gap on Orca instruction data.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
The parameter-neighborhood constraint (Case II) is not a localization test. No analysis of which weights or ranks carry safety.
No analysis of why safety is shallow in token depth. The theory concerns data similarity and context overlap, not first-token shallowness.
No deepening intervention. The constraints studied (proxy-data loss penalty, parameter-distance penalty) are evaluated only by loss gaps.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation 'tests'/T2 is wrong. The paper never measures harmful behaviour, and its 'alignment dataset' (OpenOrca) is general instruction data, so its results cannot bear on V1–V7. All experimental values are figure-only, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on harmful examples or measure harmful-request compliance/refusal.
Fine-tunes on instruction/task datasets, but does not measure harmful-request compliance/refusal.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Does not test compliant openings, suffixes, or decoding changes.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether training data or objectives cause first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate methods for spreading safety beyond the first tokens.
